notes.meaning: Bildad steps forward to give the final speech from Job's three friends. He does not try to answer Job's hard points about wicked people prospering, but instead speaks of God's unmatched majesty. Because the friends are running out of arguments, his speech is unusually short.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars argue that Bildad's speech originally included part of the next chapter, adding Job 26:5–14 to complete his thought.

notes.meaning: Bildad reminds Job that God alone holds supreme power and inspires holy reverence. The Lord maintains perfect peace and order throughout the heights of heaven. Because even the mighty angels gladly obey him without rebellion, people on earth should never presume to argue with him.

Bildad asks whether anyone can count God's armies, referring to the vast hosts of angels and stars under his command. He also asks where God's light does not shine, showing that the Lord's knowledge and care reach every corner of the earth. Since God rules over all creation and sees everything, no one can hide from him or resist his will.

Bildad asks how any human being can be justified, which means declared right and innocent before God's court. He insists that anyone born of a woman shares in human weakness and cannot claim moral purity before the Lord. Job had agreed with this general truth before, but Bildad uses it to accuse Job of having false pride.

differ.view: No one can justify themselves by good works, but believers are declared righteous in God's heavenly court solely through Christ's righteousness received by faith.
A sinner is justified by faith through Christ's sacrifice, and God's grace also enables believers to be sanctified and cleansed from inward sin.
Human beings are guilty before God's justice because of actual sins and inherit a corrupt nature from birth that only God's grace can overcome.

notes.meaning: Bildad tells Job to look up at the night sky. In comparison with God's absolute brightness and holiness, even the moon looks dim and the stars do not appear pure. If the most radiant lights in creation fall short of God's glory, human beings fall far shorter.

Bildad ends by calling mortal man a maggot and a worm, pointing to human weakness and physical decay. He means that humans are frail, earthly creatures who have no right to boast of their own goodness before God. Even so, Scripture elsewhere marvels that God lovingly cares for people despite their lowliness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew words for maggot and worm describe human beings in their lowest, weakest, and most helpless state.
